systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances?
Charles J. Courtemanche
NBER Working Paper No. 36006
November 2026
JEL No. H51, I1, I18
ABSTRACT
The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 
340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price 
Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the 
rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine 
possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to 
exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the 
effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from 
the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 
billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from 
administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative 
effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the 
pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance 
places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are 
inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.
Charles J. Courtemanche
University of Kentucky
Institute for the Study of Free Enterprise
Department of Economics
and IZA
and also NBER
courtemanche@uky.edu
1 
 
I. Introduction 
The 340B program, created by the Veterans Health Care Act (VHCA) of 1992 (Public Law 
102-585), requires pharmaceutical manufacturers to sell drugs to “covered entities” at a discount, 
with the goal being to “stretch scarce federal resources” and enhance the ability of safety-net 
providers to provide unprofitable services. Initially, the law restricted eligibility as a covered entity 
to Disproportionate-Share Hospitals (DSHs) with a Medicare DSH percentage above a threshold, 
Federally Qualified Health Centers, and Ryan White HIV/AIDS clinics. 340B pricing only applies to 
drugs prescribed at covered entities’ outpatient departments and filled at in-house pharmacies or 
external “contract pharmacies.” The pharmacy collects the usual payment from patients and insurers 
and gives it to the covered entity in exchange for a dispensing fee. The entity then orders a 
replacement drug at the discounted price, keeping the difference between the two prices – less a 
dispensing fee when contract pharmacies are used – as its margin (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 
2026). 
Two major subsequent federal laws triggered substantial expansion of the 340B program. In 
both cases, drug companies were willing to agree to these expansions because these same laws 
benefited them in other ways, such as providing access to millions of new customers. First, the 
Medicare Modernization Act (MMA) of 2003, primarily known for adding prescription drug benefits 
to Medicare through the Part D program, also applied the DSH-percentage formula used for large 
urban hospitals to rural and smaller urban hospitals. This allowed many of them to clear the 
threshold required for 340B eligibility. Second, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) of 2010, which is 
best known for its large expansions of Medicaid and private non-group insurance, added critical 
access hospitals, rural referral centers, and sole community hospitals as new categories of covered 
entities.1 It also expanded eligibility indirectly, since state Medicaid expansions under the ACA 
 
1 Additionally, the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 added children’s hospitals (Courtemanche, 2026b). 
2 
 
pushed many hospitals’ DSH percentages over the 340B threshold (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 
2026). 
HRSA’s revision of contract-pharmacy guidance also significantly expanded 340B. The 
agency’s original 1996 guidance limited covered entities to a single contract pharmacy, but a 2010 
shift removed that cap and allowed an unlimited number of pharmacies. This revised guidance was 
issued alongside the broader policy discussion surrounding the ACA and can be considered part of 
the bargaining process through which drug companies won access to a large new customer base 
while also avoiding a single-payer system (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 2026). 
Ultimately, the size of the 340B program grew from around $8 billion in 2010 (in 2025 
dollars) to $100 billion in 2025.2 Nonetheless, U.S. pharmaceutical industry profits rose from $60 
billion to $119 billion during this same time frame, outpacing the net revenues of hospitals, which 
grew from $84 billion to $94 billion.3 If one views the 340B program as a transfer from drug 
manufacturers to covered entities, this means that the program’s rapid expansion was essential to the 
hospital industry holding its net revenue steady in the face of other financing challenges. 
The rapid growth of 340B has triggered pushback from drug companies. They contend that 
the program is plagued by “duplicate discounting,” which can occur when drugs prescribed to 
Medicaid patients are eligible for both 340B discounts and Medicaid Drug Rebate Program (MDRP) 
rebates. According to the 340B statute, a manufacturer cannot be required to provide both the 340B

reported by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (2026). The 2025 number comes from Fein (2026b). 
3 Both 2010 numbers are inflation-adjusted based on the price deflator reported by the U.S. Bureau of Economic 
Analysis (2026). Information on drug company profits comes from the U.S. Census Bureau (2026). There is no 
comparable Census “corporate profits” series for hospitals since most are nonprofit. Instead, net revenues (aggregate 
revenue minus expenses) are computed by multiplying total national ‘Hospital Care’ spending (from CMS's National 
Health Expenditure Accounts; CMS Office of the Actuary, 2013) by the aggregate hospital percent margin from 
AHA/KFF analyses of Medicare cost report data (American Hospital Association, 2018; Levinson et al., 2024). In 2010, 
hospital care spending was $812.6 billion (CMS Office of the Actuary, 2013) and the margin was 7.2% (American 
Hospital Association, 2018), implying aggregate hospital net revenue of roughly $59 billion (which becomes $84 billion 
after adjusting for inflation). The latest available year of data is 2023 rather than 2025. Hospital care spending was 
roughly $1.47 trillion (calculated from CMS's reported 8.9% growth to $1.6 trillion in 2024; CMS Office of the Actuary, 
2025); aggregate total margin was 6.4% (Levinson et al., 2024). That implies aggregate hospital profit of roughly $94 
billion. 
3 
 
discount and a Medicaid rebate for the same drug fill (Public Law 102-585, 42 U.S.C. § 1396r-8). 
However, data fragmentation issues – particularly with Medicaid managed care – can make these 
cases difficult to identify in practice, leading to duplicate discounts being given in some cases. These 
challenges can also lead to diversion, which occurs when 340B pricing is given for ineligible 
patients – typically taking the form of a discount being sought by multiple covered entities for the 
same patient (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 2026). 
Since 2024, manufacturers have sought to move 340B to a rebate system, arguing that the 
existing system of upfront payments and inadequate data linkage does not allow them to prevent 
duplicate discounting (Hut, 2024; HRSA, 2026b). Covered entities have expressed concerns that a 
rebate model would give drug companies too much decision-making authority, create delays that 
could lead to cash flow problems, and impose substantial administrative costs (Courtemanche, 
2026a; HRSA, 2026b). Manufacturers were ultimately able to successfully lobby HRSA to 
implement an RMP for drugs included in the MDPNP, with the agency releasing guidance for the 
pilot in August 2026. Covered entities will no longer receive the upfront discount but instead 
purchase a drug at wholesale acquisition cost (WAC) and submit a claim to the manufacturer for a 
rebate (HRSA, 2026b). 
The MDPNP authorizes the federal government to negotiate the prices of selected high-cost 
prescription drugs with manufacturers. The negotiated prices are called “Maximum Fair Prices” 
(MFPs). The first ten drugs entered the program in 2026, with fifteen more scheduled for 2027, 
fifteen more for 2028, and twenty more slated to be added in each subsequent year (AHA News, 
2025; Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services [CMS], 2024, 2025). For 340B fills of drugs in the 
MDPNP, Medicare will only reimburse the MFP plus a small dispensing fee, lowering covered 
entity revenues. To help compensate, the statute requires that manufacturers sell covered entities 
4 
 
replacement drugs at whichever price is lower between the 340B ceiling price and the MFP 
(Courtemanche, 2026b; Santiago and Moldawer, 2025). 
Instead of building a real-time system to automatically apply the lower price at the point of 
sale, CMS relies on manufacturers to issue a retrospective discount or refund to the dispensing entity 
within 14 days of a qualifying claim (Smalldon, 2025). That retrospective, claim-by-claim 
reconciliation process creates a logistical challenge that ultimately led HRSA to agree to pilot a 
rebate system. Since HRSA created the RMP to be a solution to the practical problem caused by the 
MDPNP rather than a general reworking of the 340B program, it only applies to drugs in the 2026 
and 2027 MDPNP cohorts. However, the contentiousness of the debate raises the question of 
whether the RMP will remain connected to MFPs as the number of drugs in the MDPNP grows, 
expand to the entire 340B program as manufacturers prefer, or be short-lived as covered entities 
prefer. 
This study begins by providing a more detailed discussion of manufacturer efforts to push 
back against the growth of the 340B program, culminating in the push for a rebate model. I include 
an extended discussion of duplicate discounting, arguing that its prevalence is considerably smaller 
than manufacturer statements suggest, which has implications for the benefits of the RMP. The 
disconnect appears to largely be attributable to the drug industry using a broader definition of the 
term that also includes overlap between 340B discounts and rebates contractually negotiated with 
pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) who administer commercial drug plans and Medicare Part D. 
I then conduct a calibration analysis to project the impacts of the RMP on covered entities’ 
net revenues from 340B, holding all else constant. I also scale up these estimates to project the effect 
of implementing a rebate model for the entire 340B program. The analyses incorporate effects from 
both the rebate model itself and the fact that it will be implemented using the Beacon platform 
developed by Second Sight Solutions, whose parent company has substantial financial ties to the 
5 
 
pharmaceutical industry (Courtemanche, 2026a). Building off Courtemanche’s (2026a) study of the 
sources of value to manufacturers from utilizing Second Sight’s platforms and combining this with 
additional costs to covered entities identified by HRSA (2026b), I categorize these losses as coming 
from several sources: averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using 340B 
claims data for the purposes of influence, lobbying, physician detailing, and pharmacy targeting; 
costs related to cash flow and liquidity; and administrative and staffing costs. 
Using preferred parameter values, I project that these sources will combine to cause annual 
net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion, rising to $22.77 billion if the same model is 
expanded to all of 340B. Most of these losses will come from administrative and staffing costs 
associated with implementing the rebate model, as HRSA’s (2026b) guidance imposes restrictions 
on manufacturers that aim to guard against some of the other concerns. However, the impact would 
be larger if this guidance is ignored or inadequately enforced. Large losses – whether from low 
compliance or rebate model expansion – would raise questions about impacts on covered entities’ 
ability to provide unprofitable services and serve vulnerable populations. 
II. Background 
When the 340B program was created, administration was assigned to HRSA’s Office of 
Pharmacy Affairs. Since the VHCA gave HRSA little specific rulemaking authority, the agency has 
administered most of the program’s substance through sub-regulatory guidance rather than notice-
and-comment regulation. Manufacturers have attempted to take advantage of this ambiguity by 
imposing restrictions designed to reverse the program’s growth. This in turn triggered a flurry of 
lawsuits, with HRSA aiming to provide clarity where possible (Rogers, 2025). This section provides 
additional background about manufacturer efforts to shrink the 340B program and about the 
duplicate discounting that serves as the stated justification for these actions. 
6 
 
Beginning in 2020, Eli Lilly, AstraZeneca, Sanofi, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, and eventually 
over 20 other manufacturers began restricting 340B pricing on shipments to contract pharmacies. For 
instance, AstraZeneca would recognize only one contract pharmacy absent an in-house pharmacy, 
Sanofi and Novo Nordisk allowed more only if the covered entity supplied 340B claims data, United 
Therapeutics stopped recognizing contract pharmacies added after the third quarter of 2020, and 
Novartis limited recognition to pharmacies within 40 miles of the covered entity (Courtemanche and 
Garuccio, 2026). 
HRSA responded with an advisory opinion in December 2020 declaring the restrictions 
unlawful, which led to a wave of manufacturer lawsuits (U.S. Department of Health and Human 
Services, Office of the General Counsel, 2020). In AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP v. Becerra 
(2023), the Third Circuit held that the 340B statute does not require manufacturers to ship to an 
unlimited number of contract pharmacies. The D.C. Circuit reached a similar conclusion in May 
2024, ruling for Novartis and United Therapeutics in a consolidated case (Novartis Pharmaceuticals 
Corp. v. Johnson, 2024). These rulings in favor of manufacturers, combined with HRSA's inability 
to force compliance, spurred state legislatures to act. By August 2025, 18 states had enacted laws 
protecting contract pharmacy networks against manufacturer restrictions (ASHP News, 2025). 
Manufacturers challenged the first of these laws, Arkansas’s, but the Eighth Circuit upheld it in 
2024, ruling that Congress’ silence on contract-pharmacy distribution left room for state regulation 
(Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America v. McClain, 2024). 
Manufacturers have also increasingly required covered entities and contract pharmacies to 
route their claims data through third-party compliance platforms before 340B pricing is honored. 
The dominant platform, the Enhanced Services Platform (“ESP”), was developed by Second Sight 
Solutions, LLC. Courtemanche (2026a) documents that this company’s parent company, Berkeley 
7 
 
Research Group, has extensive ties to the pharmaceutical industry, raising conflict of interest 
questions. 
Manufacturers’ attempt to switch the 340B program from an upfront discount model to a 
rebate model represents the next step in their fight to reduce their forgone revenue from the program. 
This strategy dates back to August 2024, when Johnson & Johnson announced that a new platform 
by Second Sight, Beacon Channel Management, would administer 340B pricing for DSH hospitals 
purchasing Stelara and Xarelto as a rebate rather than a point-of-sale discount (Hut, 2024). HRSA 
directed the company to withdraw the plan, asserting that a manufacturer cannot unilaterally impose 
a rebate model without HHS approval (American Hospital Association, 2024). Johnson & Johnson 
unsuccessfully sued HHS and HRSA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, while a 
related challenge by Novartis, Eli Lilly, and Bristol Myers Squibb reached the same result on appeal 
(America’s Essential Hospitals, 2025). Together, these rulings established that an HRSA-approved 
channel would be necessary for a rebate model to move forward. This is exactly what happened next 
with HRSA’s rebate pilot. 
The process leading to the RMP began with HRSA opening an application process for 
manufacturers in mid-2025. By November, the agency had approved rebate plans from the 
manufacturers of all ten first-cohort MFP drugs (Eyman Partners, 2025). The American Hospital 
Association sued the Department of Health and Human Services and obtained a preliminary 
injunction blocking the pilot just before its planned effective date. This was upheld by the First 
Circuit Court of Appeals (Pease Bell, 2026). HRSA subsequently issued a revised version of the 
pilot via Federal Register notice on August 3, 2026 (HRSA, 2026b), with hospital groups signaling 
possible further legal challenges (American Hospital Association, 2026). 
Manufacturers have consistently framed these actions as protecting against duplicate 
discounting and diversion. In its July 2020 letter to HRSA justifying its contract-pharmacy policy, 
8 
 
AstraZeneca cited “significant increases in covered entity violations of the statutory prohibitions 
against product diversion and duplicate discounting” (AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP v. Becerra, 
Complaint, 2021). Eli Lilly offered a similar rationale for its claims-data requirement, stating that the 
data collection was “intended to stop the rampant fraud, waste, and abuse in the 340B program that 
is harming employers, state and federal governments, and patients,” and that manufacturers “can 
lawfully collect this claims data to detect fraud, abuse, and unlawful duplicate discounts” (Eli Lilly 
and Company, 2026). PhRMA has advanced the same justification for the rebate model, arguing in 
an April 2026 comment letter to HRSA that the pilot not initially being implemented left 
manufacturers with no way to prevent duplicate 340B and Medicaid discounts, that a rebate model 
“could directly benefit patients by encouraging 340B patient identification at the pharmacy or point 
of administration,” and that payers, manufacturers, and the public “are no longer obligated to 
shoulder the ever-increasing costs of rampant 340B program violations” (Pharmaceutical Research 
and Manufacturers of America, 2026). 
However, a closer look reveals that the evidence does not support claims of widespread 
statutory duplicate discounting, and that manufacturers’ interest in claims data and a rebate model 
likely reflects additional sources of value. Based on results from HRSA audits of covered entities 
combined with information on the share of Medicaid patients, Courtemanche (2026a) estimates that 
$1.9 billion of 340B purchases nationally (a relatively modest 2.3% of the annual total of $81.4 
billion) end up receiving duplicate discounts from 340B/Medicaid overlap while diversion occurs for 
an additional $1.22 billion (1.5%). The actual additional revenue pharmaceutical companies would 
make if these errors were corrected is less than these amounts, which represent the aggregate 
purchase price of all units bought with the 340B discount rather than the size of the erroneous 
discounts. In contrast, Courtemanche (2026a) estimates that other sources of value that full 
utilization of Second Sight’s platforms would create for manufacturers – including from avoiding 
9 
 
payment on valid 340B claims, building derivative data products for lobbying purposes, using the 
data to target and influence individual health care providers, and licensing the data – totals a much 
more substantial $9.33 billion per year. 
The gap between industry statements regarding duplicate discounting and the available 
evidence can be largely explained by differences in how duplicate discounting is defined. The 340B 
statute only defines duplicate discounting as the combination of a 340B discount with an MDRP 
rebate (Public Law 102-585, 42 U.S.C. § 256b(a)(5)(A)(i)). 340B discounts can occur alongside 
other discounts or rebates given by drug manufacturers, but there is no statutory basis for denying 
340B claims in such cases. For instance, in both commercial insurance and Medicare Part D, 
pharmacy benefit managers commonly negotiate confidential rebates with drug manufacturers in 
exchange for favorable formulary placement, which could include preferred tier status, absence of 
prior authorization, or preferred positioning over a competitor. These rebates are typically paid after 
the point of sale, often quarterly, and are not visible to the pharmacy or patient (Coster, 2025). 
When a drug subject to such a rebate also receives a 340B discount, manufacturers consider 
this duplicate discounting, even though it is not characterized as such by the law. A white paper by 
IQVIA – a company whose customer base is mostly drug and biotech companies (Umbrex, 2026) – 
makes this clear by stating that “products dispensed to a 340B patient, should not be subject to a 
payor (commercial or state) rebate,” and describing such rebates as resulting in “significant financial 
losses for manufacturers” (Singh, 2023, pp. 3–4). Using the expansive definition of duplicate 
discounting favored by the pharmaceutical industry, IQVIA estimates it to be $34 to $37.5 billion 
per year (Singh, 2023), representing almost 30% of the study’s estimated size of 340B.4 As a percent 
of the program, this is about 13 times larger than Courtemanche’s (2026a) estimate. This stark 
difference is not surprising; whereas the statutory definition limits duplicate discounting to 
 
4 IQVIA computes a larger program size than HRSA because it uses WAC pricing rather than 340B pricing. 
10 
 
Medicaid, which covers only 18% of the U.S. population, the expansive definition also includes 
commercial insurance (66%) and Medicare (19%) (Bunch and Ketema, 2025). 
III. Methods and Results 
This section aims to quantify the losses to covered entities from the RMP, holding all else 
constant. Drawing on the discussion in Courtemanche (2026a), t

number of contract pharmacy relationships has doubled since then (Fein, 2026a), 
suggesting that a better estimate of the current percentage for contract pharmacies would be 34%. 
This implies an average percentage liquidity cost – given by 0.19% * 0.66 + 0.03% * 0.34 – of 
0.1356%. Recall that the WAC value of the $100 billion of 340B purchases in 2025 was $179.5 
billion, which translates to $9.873 billion after multiplying by the 5.5% share of the 2026 and 2027 
cohorts of MDPNP drugs. Therefore, the liquidity cost comes to 0.1356% of $9.873 billion, which is 
$13.4 million. As a sensitivity analysis, using the 17% contract pharmacy figure from 2021 would 
yield an average percentage liquidity cost of 0.1628%, which translates to $16.1 million. 
Alternatively, a same-sized change in contract pharmacy percentage in the other direction – to 51% – 
would imply an average percentage liquidity cost of 0.1084%, leading to $10.7 million. Since the 
25 
 
liquidity cost should scale relatively linearly as the share of 340B drugs using a rebate model 
increases, I estimate the effect of full implementation of the rebate model using Beacon by 
multiplying these numbers by 100 / 5.5. This yields a central estimate of $243.6 million and a range 
of $194.5 million to $292.7 million. 
Administrative and Staffing Costs 
HRSA (2026b) also acknowledges that covered entities will incur administrative and staffing 
costs from the RMP. These costs will include new claims-submission workflows, data reconciliation, 
and dispute handling. HRSA estimates this cost to be a total of $523.34 million per year across 
15,249 covered entities, for an average of $34,320 per entity. However, covered entity 
representatives who submitted comments claim that these annual costs will be higher, ranging from 
$30,000 to over $200,000 for staffing alone (Hananoki and Franco, 2026). The midpoint of this 
range implies total costs across all 15,249 covered entities of $1.75 billion per year. There will also 
be one-time administrative and information technology (IT) costs associated with implementation, 
though HRSA’s notice requires manufacturers to bear all costs for the IT platform (Dykema, 2026). 
For this reason, and because startup costs will pale in comparison to annual costs in the long run, I 
ignore startup costs in my analysis. To calibrate annual administrative and staffing costs, I use 
HRSA’s $523.34 million estimate as the low end of the range, covered entities’ $1.75 billion as the 
high end, and the average of these – $1.14 billion – as the central (preferred) value. 
Extrapolating to the costs of implementation of the rebate model using Beacon for the entire 
340B program is not straightforward because there are likely to be at least some economies of scale, 
which means that a linear projection would likely overstate the losses. I therefore use an inverse 
process to that used to model diminishing returns above, since the predicted effect of the RMP is 
known rather than the predicted effect of a rebate model for the entire program. This means solving 
for a in the equation $1.14 billion = ($5.5 billion)a, which yields 0.9298. Therefore, the cost from 
26 
 
full implementation at central parameter values comes to ($100 billion)0.9298, which is $16.9 
billion. The low end of the range is given by solving for a in $523.34 million = ($5.5 billion)a, 
which gives 0.8951, and then computing ($100 billion)0.8951, which is $7.02 billion. Similarly, 
determining the high end requires solving $1.75 billion = ($5.5 billion)a, which is 0.9489, and then 
calculating ($100 billion)0.9489, which gives $27.4 billion. 
Total Annual Losses 
 We are now ready to add together the different projected sources of covered entity losses 
from the RMP as well as full implementation of a rebate model using Beacon for the entire 340B 
program. Table 5 reports the estimates for the RMP, displaying the central estimate of each source of 
losses along with the highest and lowest estimates from sensitivity analyses. Using central parameter 
values, I predict total annual covered entity lost net revenue from the RMP to be $1.5 billion. The 
low end of the range is $702 million and the high end is $2.37 billion. Table 6 reports analogous 
estimates for full implementation. I project that the expansion of the rebate model to the entire 340B 
program would lead to annual net revenue losses of $22.77 billion, with a range from $10.04 billion 
to $37.59 billion. In all columns in both tables, the substantial majority of the losses – between 70% 
and 76% – come from administrative and staffing costs. 
 

27 
 
 
IV. Conclusion 
For drugs in the MDPNP, 340B covered entities are eligible for the lower of the MFP and 
340B ceiling price. The lack of a system to identify and charge the lower price in real time creates 
implementation challenges. This, combined with longstanding manufacturer concerns about 
duplicate discounting, led HRSA to develop a pilot to implement a 340B rebate model for MDPNP 
drugs. Covered entities have objected to the RMP due to concerns about drug companies being given 
the power to approve or deny claims, cash flow challenges from delayed payments, administrative 
costs, and the conflict of interest created by the RMP’s claims submission platform being run by a 
company with connections to the pharmaceutical industry. After legal challenges, HRSA released an 
official notice for a revised version of the pilot that aims to address some of these concerns in 
August 2026. This study asks two questions. First, how will the RMP affect covered entities’ net 
revenues from the 340B program? Second, what would be the impact of implementing the same 
rebate model for all of 340B, rather than just the 22 drugs in the first two MDPNP cohorts? 
I begin with a section that provides background information about manufacturers’ efforts to 
push back against the growth of the 340B program. I examine the premise behind these efforts: that 
duplicate discounting by covered entities is widespread. I argue that a major source of the gap 
between industry statements and the available evidence is that drug companies define duplicate 
discounting much more broadly than the 340B statute. Courtemanche (2026a) suggests that 

28 
 
manufacturers’ interest in the rebate model likely extends beyond preventing statutory duplicate 
discounting, as requiring covered entities to submit claims data through an industry-connected 
platform creates other sources of value that are much more substantial than the benefit from stopping 
duplicate discounting by the statutory definition. 
I then turn to the quantitative analyses, allowing effects to come both from the rebate model 
itself and manufacturers’ ability to use the data collected to implement it in ways that can shrink the 
340B program. More specifically, covered entity losses can come from averted duplicate discounts; 
denial of valid claims; manufacturers using 340B claims data for the purposes of influence, 
lobbying, physician detailing, and pharmacy targeting; costs related to cash flow and liquidity; and 
administrative and staffing costs. Based on preferred parameter values, I estimate annual net revenue 
losses of $1.5 billion from the RMP and $22.77 billion from expanding the rebate model to the full 
program. The majority of these losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, but losses 
from other sources have the potential to be much higher if HRSA’s guidance for manufacturers is 
ignored, not enforced, or not included in a scaled-up rebate model. One specific concern is that 
compliance may be high during the initial pilot period as manufacturers aim to convince HRSA that 
the rebate model is working, but then worsen once the model has expanded beyond the point where 
it would be impossible to reverse. 
Losses of $22.77 billion would eliminate 32% of net revenues from 340B and, strikingly, 
24% of the combined net revenues of all hospitals in the U.S.6 Losses of this magnitude have the 
potential to significantly affect access to care. In their review of the scholarly literature on 340B, 
Courtemanche and Garuccio (2026) document substantial evidence that covered entities use at least 
some of their 340B revenue to maintain or expand provision of services to vulnerable populations. 
According to the Chartis Center for Rural Health (2026), 417 rural hospitals are vulnerable to

29 
 
closure, 448 have dropped chemotherapy in the past decade, and 331 have dropped obstetrics. 
Therefore, a loss of 340B net revenue of the magnitude found in this study would likely lead to 
closures of unprofitable departments and, in some cases, entire hospitals. 
Adding to the concern are two other developments that have the potential to substantially 
harm covered entity finances. The first is the MDPNP itself, which lowers covered entity costs when 
MFPs are below the 340B ceiling price but reduces revenues by lowering Medicare reimbursement 
rates to MFP plus a dispensing fee, which in turn will likely trigger a downward adjustment in 
commercial rates. Courtemanche (2026b) computes that the revenue reduction – which occurs across 
a broader base of drugs and payers – will far outweigh the cost reduction, harming covered entity 
finances on net. 
Second, CMS has proposed a 2027 Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) rule that 
would reduce 340B Part B hospital reimbursement from 6% above average sales price to 33.4% 
below. CMS estimates a $4.55 billion reduction in Medicare drug payments from this change, which 
means an equivalent reduction in covered entity revenue. This would be accompanied by a budget-
neutral increase in non-drug OPPS payments that would be spread across all OPPS hospitals, 
whereas only covered entities would bear the losses (CMS, 2026). 
These other developments highlight the importance of viewing the challenges facing covered 
entities holistically rather than separately. Unfortunately, it is not feasible with available data to 
develop a single comprehensive model that incorporates the interactive effects of these different 
forces. The impacts predicted by my analysis were computed in “all else equal” fashion based on a 
2025 baseline. Changes to payment rules would inevitably influence effect sizes. With that said, this 
influence is somewhat limited by three factors. First, since Part B drugs were not included in the 
2026 and 2027 MDPNP cohorts, the proposed OPPS payment changes are not relevant for the 
projections about the RMP – though they are for the projections about switching the entire 340B 
30 
 
program to a rebate model. Second, conversely, MDPNP payment changes are relevant for the RMP 
but not for extrapolation to the rest of the 340B program, as drugs not in the MDPNP are unaffected. 
Third, there is considerable policy uncertainty surrounding whether the OPPS changes will be 
implemented, whether the MDPNP will expand as planned, and whether the rebate model will scale 
up with the MDPNP if it does. Therefore, it is unclear whether incorporating all these potential 
changes into a single model would be desirable even if it were feasible. 
Modeling details aside, the fact that the 340B program faces pressures from several 
directions underscores the importance of taking a holistic view of these challenges when evaluating 
the merits of any single revenue-reducing policy change. To illustrate, when viewed in isolation, one 
might argue that covered entity losses from the RMP are relatively modest. However, this argument 
becomes weaker once observers recognize that covered entities face multiple forces putting 
substantial downward pressure on 340B net revenue. When viewed in this manner, even seemingly 
modest losses from the RMP could be consequential for safety-net providers struggling to remain 
financially viable. Similarly, once the pressures covered entities already face from the MDPNP and 
potential expansion of the rebate model is understood, implementing the OPPS rate cuts may appear 
less desirable. Alternatively, policymakers could consider offsetting covered entities’ losses with an 
additional policy lever such as increased disproportionate share funds. While identifying the ideal 
bundle of policies is beyond the scope of this paper, taking a holistic view would give policymakers 
a better chance of achieving their objectives while minimizing unintended consequences. 
Another relevant aspect of this study’s results for optimal policy is that the majority of 
projected losses from the rebate model come from administrative and staffing costs. In contrast to 
other sources of losses such as averted duplicate discounting, drug manufacturers do not benefit 
when covered entities incur higher administrative and staffing costs. This means that manufacturer 
gains from the RMP are smaller than covered entity losses, implying a negative net effect of the 
31 
 
rebate model. In a full social welfare calculation, employment created by the added administrative 
work would be counted as an offsetting force, but employment effects are not an objective of the 
RMP and would not be expected to outweigh the efficiency loss. 
The analyses in this paper also have implications for the broader policy debate over 340B. 
First, because the program faces several simultaneous revenue pressures, evaluating each policy 
change in isolation is likely to understate its consequences for covered entities and the populations 
they serve. Second, the distinction between statutory and non-statutory duplicate discounting matters 
for interpreting prevalence estimates. HRSA’s (2026b) guidance cites statistics from pharmaceutical-
industry-funded studies using the expansive definition of duplicate discounting, which my analysis 
suggests overstates the prevalence of statutory duplicate discounting by an order of magnitude. It 
seems unlikely that HRSA’s citation of these numbers was meant to give tacit approval of the 
expansive definition, as the agency has always clearly defined duplicate discounting in the statutory 
sense. Instead, HRSA likely quoted these numbers simply because they are the most publicized 
estimates. Independent, transparent estimates based on the statutory definition would help inform 
this debate. For instance, HRSA reports results from its audits in terms of the percentage of covered 
entities with at least one violation; releasing information on the extent of the violations where at least 
one occurs would be more informative. 
Finally, if it becomes clear that the rebate model will become permanent – either for just 
MDPNP drugs or for the entire 340B program – attention should go towards minimizing its costs. 
This takes two forms. First, the estimates in this study depend critically on the extent to which 
HRSA’s restrictions on manufacturers are followed and enforced. Policymakers should therefore 
prioritize monitoring and enforcement of these restrictions and ensure that comparable safeguards 
accompany any expansion of the rebate model. Second, because administrative and staffing costs 
account for most of the projected losses, policymakers could consider offsetting them through 
32 
 
government or manufacturer funding or modifying implementation details to reduce them. The 340B 
program is at a critical juncture, and the cumulative effects of these policy changes on safety-net 
providers warrant careful consideration.
